leaks.title: Three positions carry 86% of all losses
leaks.fix: Set a hard cash ceiling per position — ₹24,794, the size of one average win — and work quantity backwards from it so no single idea can do this again.

leaks.title: Losers run, winners get cut short
leaks.evidence: An average winner books ₹24,794 (78.3%) while an average loser gives back ₹73,624 (−32.8%). 33 of 74 positions ended red.
leaks.fix: Decide the exit before the entry: −30% of premium on options and −8% of position value on futures and stocks. Applied across this period that holds back roughly ₹10.45L.

leaks.title: Leveraged positions left without a stop
leaks.evidence: HDFCBANK26APRFUT −₹600 (−5.0% of notional) · PFC26APRFUT −₹600 (−5.0% of notional) · NIFTY25SEPFUT −₹6.16L (−10.0% of notional).
leaks.fix: On futures, 2% of notional is already a full-size loss. Fix the stop as a cash amount first, then choose lots — not the other way round.

leaks.title: Bought options held until the premium was gone
leaks.evidence: 5 option buys exited below a tenth of cost: TCS22MAR3800CE −₹3.09L · MIDCPNIFTY2410811000CE −₹4,312 · NIFTY22JAN18000CE −₹428 · BANKNIFTY24OCT52000PE −₹294.
leaks.fix: Treat premium as a stop that decays on its own: cut at 30–40% down and never carry a long option through the last two sessions hoping for a move.

leaks.title: A 4-trade losing streak with no circuit breaker
leaks.evidence: The run cost −₹3.10L before it ended on its own.
leaks.fix: Cap the day at ₹49,588 of loss. Hitting it means the market isn't paying today and the terminal gets closed.

leaks.title: Losers exited in instalments
leaks.fix: One decision, one order. Selling a loser in pieces is a way of not deciding, and the piece left behind is always the one that falls further.

leaks.title: Squared off by the broker 2 times
leaks.fix: Set an alarm 20 minutes before the close and flatten intraday positions yourself. A broker-forced exit takes whatever price the market offers.

leaks.title: Penalties for running too close to the margin
leaks.fix: Keep 20% headroom over required margin. Shortfall penalties are money lost without any market risk taken.

rules.rule: Cut any bought option at −30% of premium
rules.why: Worth about ₹8.81L over the trades in this file.

rules.rule: Stop futures and stock positions at −8% of position value
rules.why: Worth roughly ₹1.65L on the same trades.
One average win. Work the quantity backwards from this number, not from available margin.

rules.rule: Two losses in a row ends the session
rules.why: Trades taken right after a loss are your weakest set.
Your worst streak ran 4 trades before stopping by itself.

rules.rule: Exit a loser in one order
rules.why: Partial exits on losing positions consistently cost more than the first exit would have.

rules.rule: Flat or converted 20 minutes before the close
rules.why: Removes auto square-off fees and the exit price that comes with them.

rules.rule: Skip any setup with a target under 1.0%
rules.why: Round-trip costs run about 0.07%; anything thinner works for the broker, not you.

rules.rule: Write entry, stop and target before the order goes in
rules.why: Every leak above traces back to an exit that was never decided in advance.

report.diagnosis: You pick direction well — 55% of positions close green — but a single loss erases 3.0 wins. This is an exit problem, not an entry problem.

traits.name: Tail risk blindness
traits.now: Just three trades account for 86% of everything you lost.
traits.why: Most trades feel controlled, so risk feels controlled. But the damage is concentrated in a few moments when discipline slipped. Those few trades decide the year, and they are the ones that never get reviewed.
traits.ideal: No single trade can lose more than a fixed cash amount, set before entry. The worst trades get reviewed first.

traits.name: The one-big-loss problem
traits.now: Your worst trade lost ₹11.55L, about 47 average wins.
traits.why: A single large loss usually starts as a normal trade that was never stopped out. Each small move against you felt too small to act on, until the total was too big to accept.
traits.ideal: The maximum loss on any trade is about one average win. Anything bigger is treated as a process failure, not bad luck.

traits.name: Inconsistent sizing
traits.now: Your position sizes vary wildly: the spread is 4.5× the average size.
traits.why: When size is decided by feel, conviction and mood set the bet. Your biggest positions end up where you felt most certain, which is not the same as where your edge is greatest.
traits.ideal: Position size comes from a formula: risk per trade divided by distance to stop.

traits.name: Need to be right
traits.now: A high win rate (55%) paired with small winners and large losers.
traits.why: For some traders a winning trade matters more as a sign of being right than as money. Losses get held so they don't have to be admitted, and wins are taken quickly to feel right.
traits.ideal: Measure success by money made per unit of risk, not by how often you're right.

traits.name: Big bets, bad outcomes
traits.now: Your largest positions lost ₹16.41L with a 39% win rate.
traits.why: Big positions are usually taken when confidence is high, and high confidence often follows recent success or a strong story. Certainty feels like information, but it is just a feeling.
traits.ideal: Larger size is earned by a setup's track record, not by how convinced you feel today.

traits.name: Stop-loss aversion
traits.now: 64% of losing trades went beyond a 10% loss.
traits.why: Placing a stop means accepting in advance that you might be wrong. Many traders avoid it to keep the possibility of being right alive.
traits.ideal: A stop is part of every order. A trade without a stop is not taken.

traits.name: Action bias
traits.now: You average 4.1 trades per trading day, and the average trade loses money.
traits.why: Sitting still feels like missing out, and watching the screen without trading feels like wasted time. So trades are taken to have done something, not because the edge is there.
traits.ideal: Not trading is a valid decision. Many good trading days have zero trades.

traits.name: Theta denial
traits.now: 5 bought options lost almost all their value through decay.
traits.why: An option that isn't moving feels like it is waiting. In reality it is losing value every hour, and the loss is invisible until it is large.
traits.ideal: Bought options have a time stop as well as a price stop.

more.name: Loss aversion
more.now: Your average loss (₹73,624) is 3.0× your average win (₹24,794).
more.why: Closing a loser makes the loss real, so the mind keeps it open for one more candle. A winner feels like something to protect, so it gets banked early. The pain of losing weighs roughly twice the pleasure of an equal gain, and your exits reflect that imbalance.
more.ideal: Losses are closed at a level decided before entry, and winners are given at least as much room as losers.

more.name: Volatility denial
more.now: 3 futures positions lost 5% or more of notional value.
more.why: Leverage hides risk. A 5% move feels small in percentage terms, but on a futures position it can equal weeks of gains. The brain judges the move, not the exposure.
more.ideal: Futures risk is measured in cash per lot. The stop is set so a full stop-out is a normal, survivable loss.

more.name: Anchoring to the entry price
more.now: 64% of your losing trades went more than 10% against you before you closed them.
more.why: The price you paid becomes the reference point for the whole trade. Every exit below it feels like "selling at a loss", so you wait for the market to return to your number, even though the market doesn't know it exists.
more.ideal: Exit decisions are made relative to the trade idea being right or wrong, not relative to your entry price.

more.name: Small-loss reluctance
more.now: Hardly any trades close near breakeven (0%); losers are allowed to grow instead.
more.why: Taking a small loss feels like admitting a mistake immediately. Waiting feels free. But a trader who never takes small losses is a trader who takes large ones.
more.ideal: Many trades end as small losses or scratches. That is what cutting early looks like in the data.

more.name: Hope as a strategy
more.now: 5 bought options were held until they were worth less than a tenth of their price, costing ₹3.14L.
more.why: Once a position is deep in the red, closing it feels pointless because "the damage is done". Holding on costs nothing emotionally and keeps a small chance of rescue alive, so hope quietly replaces the exit plan.
more.ideal: Every bought option has a premium stop. A trade that hits it is closed, whatever it might do tomorrow.

more.name: Scattershot selection
more.now: You traded 28 different underlyings, 18 of them only once.
more.why: Jumping between many names means never building a feel for any of them. Each new name is a fresh start, which is exciting, but excitement is not an edge.
more.ideal: A short, stable watchlist of instruments you know well.

more.name: Auto-pilot exits
more.now: Your broker closed your intraday positions 2 times because you hadn't.
more.why: Letting the broker square off means no exit decision was made. Either the trade was forgotten or closing it felt too painful.
more.ideal: Every intraday position is closed by you before the cut-off, at a time you choose.

more.name: Process over outcome gap
more.now: Across 74 trades, the average trade loses ₹19,095.
more.why: Over a large number of trades, luck mostly cancels out. A negative average across many trades is a process problem, not a bad patch.
more.ideal: The process is changed in one specific way, then measured over the next 30–50 trades.

more.name: Novelty seeking
more.now: You traded 28 different underlyings in this period.
more.why: New instruments bring fresh excitement and the sense that this one will be different. Variety feels like opportunity but usually spreads attention too thin.
more.ideal: New instruments are added only after they are tested on paper.

more.name: Margin brinkmanship
more.now: You were charged 1 margin or collateral penalty.
more.why: Running close to the margin limit means using every rupee available. It feels efficient but leaves no room for error, and the penalties are losses taken without any trade.
more.ideal: At least 20% of required margin is kept free at all times.

more.name: Directional stubbornness
more.now: You trade calls more (70% of options) but they lose ₹14.52L; puts made ₹7.25L.
more.why: A bias about market direction quietly shapes which side you choose. The side you prefer is not the side that pays you, but preference wins because it matches your view of the world.
more.ideal: Direction is chosen by the setup on the chart, and each side's results are reviewed separately.

more.name: Outcome bias
more.now: You're right 55% of the time, yet the average trade loses money.
more.why: Being right often feels like proof of a good process. But money is made from the size of wins against losses. Judging a trade only by whether it worked hides the problem.
more.ideal: Each trade is reviewed on its risk/reward and execution, not only on whether it won.

net.ideal: Net P&L after costs is the only number that pays. Judge every change to your trading by its effect here.

gross.ideal: Gross P&L should comfortably exceed costs; if it barely does, trade less, not more.

costs.now: Costs were 1% of what your winners made.
costs.ideal: Costs under 15–20% of gross profit. Fewer trades with larger targets get you there.

winrate.ideal: Win rate only matters alongside payoff. 40% with 2:1 winners beats 60% with 1:2.

payoff.now: Average win is 0.34× the average loss.
payoff.ideal: A payoff above 1.5 gives room for a normal win rate to be profitable.

avgwin.ideal: Winners run to a planned target instead of being taken at the first sign of profit.

avgloss.ideal: Losers closed at a pre-set stop, so the average loss is smaller than the average win.

pf.ideal: A profit factor above 1.3 after costs is a sustainable edge.

worst.now: Your worst trade was ₹11.55L, about 46.6 average wins.
worst.ideal: The worst trade is no bigger than one or two average wins.

costsPanel.ideal: Every trade expected to make several times its cost.

leaks.ideal: Leaks are fixed one at a time, starting with the most expensive.

curve.now: At the worst point you were ₹19.99L below your peak.
curve.ideal: A steady upward slope with shallow dips; deep drops mean risk per trade is too high.

instrument.ideal: Capital goes to the instrument where your results are best, not where the action is.

afterwinloss.now: After a loss your next trade averages −₹7,672; after a win, −₹28,864.

diagnosis.ideal: A positive average trade after costs, held steady over hundreds of trades.

rules.now: Rules built from your own mistakes.

patterns.ideal: Do more of what works, pause what consistently doesn't.

psych.ideal: Awareness first; then one rule per habit, tested for a month.

stopsOpt.now: 5 bought options were held to near zero.
stopsOpt.ideal: Bought options exit at a fixed share of premium, usually 30–40% down.

stopsLin.ideal: Stops sized so a full stop-out is a normal loss.

weekday.ideal: If one expiry day stands out as losing, avoid holding into it.

premium.now: Results by the premium you paid.
premium.ideal: Pick strikes for probability and liquidity, not price.

expiryType.now: 45% of your options were weekly contracts.
expiryType.ideal: Match the expiry to how long your idea needs.

callPut.ideal: Trade the side the setup shows; review each side separately.

entryDow.now: Friday is your weakest entry day.
entryDow.ideal: Size down on days that consistently lose until you know why.

entryHour.ideal: Trade the hours where your record is best; sit out the rest.

hold.ideal: Winners held at least as long as losers.

busyDay.now: Results by how many trades you made that day.
busyDay.ideal: A daily trade limit. Quality drops as the count rises.

direction.ideal: Both sides traded when the setup is there.

month.ideal: Most months profitable, with small losing months.

size.ideal: Size follows a formula, not conviction.

style.ideal: Holding period decided at entry, never changed because a trade is losing.

lossDepth.ideal: Most losses small, almost none deep. Deep losses mean stops weren't used.

worstU.now: The names that cost you most.
worstU.ideal: Repeat losers go on a pause list.

bestU.now: The names that pay you most.
